ai.definition: Nuclear fusion power plants are facilities designed to produce electricity by replicating the process that powers the sun. In these reactors, atomic nuclei combine under extreme temperatures and pressures to release a significant amount of energy.
ai.howItWorks: Fusion reactions can be achieved through two primary methods: magnetic confinement (e.g., tokamaks) and inertial confinement (e.g., laser fusion). In magnetic confinement, a plasma is contained in a toroidal chamber using powerful magnetic fields. Inertial confinement uses intense lasers or particle beams to compress fuel pellets, causing them to fuse.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the global energy crisis by providing a clean and virtually limitless source of power that does not produce greenhouse gases or long-lived radioactive waste like traditional nuclear fission reactors do.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves constructing highly specialized facilities capable of maintaining conditions necessary for fusion reactions. This includes precise control systems, advanced materials, and complex engineering challenges related to heat management and plasma stability.
ai.buildProcess: Construction begins with site selection and environmental impact assessments. The reactor design is then developed in collaboration with international partners before moving into the fabrication phase where components are manufactured according to stringent specifications. Testing and commissioning follow to ensure safety and performance standards are met.
ai.costDrivers: High initial capital costs, long development timelines, and technological uncertainties contribute significantly to the overall expense of building nuclear fusion power plants.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: While significant progress has been made in recent years, commercial-scale fusion reactors are still several decades away from widespread deployment. Current projects like ITER aim to demonstrate scientific feasibility but face numerous technical hurdles before becoming economically viable alternatives to fossil fuels.
ai.regulation: Regulations surrounding nuclear fusion power plants will likely be stringent due to the potential for radioactive materials and safety concerns associated with handling high-energy plasmas. International cooperation and standardization efforts are expected to play a crucial role in establishing regulatory frameworks.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving sustained net energy gain, managing plasma instabilities, and developing materials that can withstand extreme conditions without degradation. Safety risks involve the potential for accidents during operation or decommissioning processes.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given current technological limitations and high development costs. However, if successful, fusion power could provide a highly profitable source of clean energy in the long term.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include improved confinement techniques, new materials science advancements, and enhanced computational modeling to optimize reactor designs. International collaboration remains key for overcoming technical challenges and accelerating progress towards commercialization.

glossary.def: A state of matter where atoms are ionized, resulting in a mixture of free electrons and positively charged ions.
A toroidal-shaped device used for magnetic confinement fusion to contain plasma within a doughnut-shaped vacuum chamber.
A method of achieving nuclear fusion by rapidly compressing and heating fuel targets using high-intensity lasers or particle beams.

subsystems.name: Confinement core
subsystems.role: the machine that holds and heats the fusing plasma — a magnetic torus, a stellarator, or a laser-driven target chamber.

subsystems.name: Blanket and heat-transfer loop
subsystems.role: a lithium-bearing wall that absorbs the fusion neutrons, breeds tritium and carries the captured heat away.
parts: coolant channels (helium, water or molten salt)

subsystems.name: Tritium plant
subsystems.role: recovers bred tritium, separates it from exhaust gas and returns it to the fuel injectors.

subsystems.name: Exhaust and divertor
subsystems.role: strips helium 'ash' and heat from the plasma edge before it reaches the walls.

subsystems.name: Shielding, vacuum and containment
subsystems.role: protects equipment and people from neutrons and keeps the plasma chamber at near-vacuum.

subsystems.name: Balance of plant
subsystems.role: turns blanket heat into grid electricity, like a conventional thermal station.
parts: steam generator or supercritical CO2 cycle

subsystems.name: Remote maintenance
subsystems.role: handles components that become radioactive through neutron bombardment and cannot be touched.

buildSteps.title: Qualify the materials
buildSteps.detail: Candidate steels and tungsten alloys are irradiated in test reactors and ion beams for years to prove they survive a plant lifetime of neutron damage.

buildSteps.title: Build the confinement machine
buildSteps.detail: Magnets are wound from superconducting cable or a target chamber is assembled, then the vacuum vessel is welded around them to millimetre tolerances.

buildSteps.title: Install the first wall and blanket
buildSteps.detail: Breeder modules and plasma-facing tiles are fitted inside the vessel, with coolant plumbing for every module.

buildSteps.title: Add shielding and the tritium plant
buildSteps.detail: Bioshield concrete or steel goes up around the machine, and the tritium processing building is connected as a sealed, monitored system.

buildSteps.title: Connect the balance of plant
buildSteps.detail: Heat exchangers, turbine hall and switchyard are tied to the blanket coolant loop and commissioned on conventional heat sources.

buildSteps.title: Commission with hydrogen
buildSteps.detail: The plant runs first on hydrogen and deuterium only, learning plasma control and machine behaviour without radioactive fuel.

buildSteps.title: Introduce deuterium–tritium fuel
buildSteps.detail: Tritium is added, neutron output rises, the blanket starts breeding, and the tritium inventory must balance or the plant cannot keep running.

buildSteps.title: First electricity to the grid
buildSteps.detail: Heat from the blanket drives the turbine and the plant exports power — the step no fusion device has yet taken.

buildSteps.title: Decommissioning and waste route
buildSteps.detail: Activated components must be stored and eventually recycled or disposed of under nuclear regulations.

prerequisites.tech: High-field superconducting magnets or high-gain inertial targets
prerequisites.why: they set the size, cost and achievable plasma performance of the whole plant.
a single laser shot reached net gain in 2022, but no device has produced sustained fusion power with a practical fuel cycle.
fusion neutrons damage materials far faster than fission neutrons, and no qualified alloy exists for a plant's full service life.

prerequisites.tech: Tritium breeding and handling at scale
prerequisites.why: a plant must breed its own tritium from lithium and hold a large, well-contained inventory.
blanket and divertor modules will need replacement every few years by robots, because radiation rules out human access.
regulators have no established framework for tritium inventories, activated waste or plant siting.

pathway.milestone: ITER assembly in France; laser ignition demonstrated at a US national facility in 2022; JET's deuterium–tritium record before it shut down in 2023
pathway.unlocks: physics data at power-plant scale and lessons for the next generation of machines.

pathway.milestone: pilot plants aiming to generate net electricity, built by national programmes and privately funded ventures
pathway.unlocks: proof that heat can be extracted and converted to power reliably.

pathway.milestone: demonstration plants with a closed tritium fuel cycle and replaceable blanket modules
pathway.unlocks: self-sufficient fuel, realistic maintenance schedules and cost data for utilities.

pathway.milestone: first commercial fleets, supported by lithium and tritium supply chains and a licensing regime
pathway.unlocks: firm, low-carbon baseload power — provided materials, fuel breeding and remote maintenance all perform as designed.
